title: Databases from Node
intro: Almost every Node backend talks to a database, and most production incidents involve it: exhausted pools, slow queries, double inserts, lost updates. Interviewers want to see that you know what happens between your await and the database — connections, transactions, locks and error codes — and that you push correctness into the database instead of hoping JavaScript checks are enough. Expect practical code questions with pg, mysql2, Prisma or Mongoose.

questions.title: Connection pooling
questions.question: Why do we use a connection pool when talking to a database from Node? How do you size it, and what does pool exhaustion look like?
questions.short: Opening a DB connection is expensive (TCP, TLS, auth, and in Postgres a whole server process per connection), and one connection can only run one query at a time. A pool keeps a fixed set of open connections and lends them out per query, so requests reuse them and concurrency is capped. Size it small — often 10–20 per Node process — and make sure pool size times number of instances stays below the database's connection limit. Exhaustion looks like requests waiting for a connection: rising latency, timeouts like "timeout exceeded when trying to connect", while the DB itself may look idle. The usual cause is leaked clients or slow queries holding connections.
questions.simple: A pool is like a small fleet of taxis waiting at the stand. Riders take a taxi and bring it back. If people never return taxis, the queue at the stand grows forever.

list: Connecting costs milliseconds to tens of milliseconds; a simple query can take under a millisecond. Reusing connections removes that overhead.
A connection runs one query at a time. Node is single-threaded but issues many queries concurrently, so it needs several connections.
The database has a hard limit (`max_connections` in Postgres, 100 by default). Each Postgres connection is a separate backend process using memory. The pool caps how many you use.
Bigger is not faster. The DB has a fixed number of CPU cores and disks; too many concurrent queries cause contention and context switching.
Budget: `pool.max × processes × instances` + migrations + admin tools must stay below the DB limit. 20 pods × 4 cluster workers × 10 = 800 connections — too many for most Postgres servers.
When you need many app instances, put a connection pooler like PgBouncer (transaction mode) or a managed proxy in front of the database.
Serverless functions each create their own pool; use `max: 1`–`2` per instance plus an external pooler.
Latency jumps for all endpoints at once, even simple ones.
`pool.waitingCount` grows; `pool.idleCount` is 0; `pool.totalCount` equals `max`.
Errors like `timeout exceeded when trying to connect` (only if `connectionTimeoutMillis` is set — otherwise requests hang).
The DB shows few active queries but many connections "idle in transaction", which points to leaks or long transactions.

explain.note: Export pool metrics (total, idle, waiting) to your monitoring. A waiting count above zero for long periods is the earliest warning sign.

anim.title: Requests share a pool of 3 connections

steps.note: The pool allows at most 3 connections. They are created lazily and then kept open for reuse.
Three /report requests arrive. Each pool.query borrows one connection.
Requests 4 and 5 arrive. No connection is free, so they wait in the pool's queue. No new connection is opened past max.
req1's query finishes and pool.query releases c1. The pool hands it straight to req4.
req2 and req3 finish. c2 goes to req5, c3 becomes idle.
All done. Every connection is back and ready for reuse, no reconnect cost.
Now /leaky is called. It checks out a client manually with pool.connect().
It responds but never calls client.release(). c1 is stuck as "in use" forever.
Two more /leaky calls leak c2 and c3. The pool is empty although nothing is running.
Every new request now waits. Latency rises everywhere, even on endpoints that do not leak.
After connectionTimeoutMillis (2 s) each waiter fails with "timeout exceeded when trying to connect". Without that option they hang forever.

followups.q: How do you find a connection leak?
followups.a: Watch pool.totalCount/idleCount/waitingCount, look for 'idle in transaction' sessions in pg_stat_activity, and audit every pool.connect() for a release() in a finally block. In tests, assert the pool is fully idle after each test.

followups.q: Should each request open its own connection instead?
followups.a: No. That pays the connection cost on every request and can blow past the DB connection limit under load. The only exception is serverless with an external pooler.

followups.q: What about Node cluster or multiple pods?
followups.a: Each process has its own pool, so total connections multiply. Size per-process pools with the whole fleet in mind.

mistakes: Setting max: 100 per process "to be safe" and exhausting the database.
Using pool.connect() without releasing in finally.
Leaving connectionTimeoutMillis at 0, so exhaustion shows up as hangs instead of errors.
Creating a new Pool per request or per module import.

questions.title: SQL injection and parameterized queries
questions.question: How does SQL injection happen in Node code, and how do you prevent it with pg or mysql2?
questions.short: Injection happens when user input is concatenated into the SQL text, so the input can change the query's structure. The fix is parameterized queries: the SQL text has placeholders ($1 in pg, ? in mysql2) and values are sent separately, so they are always treated as data. Placeholders only work for values, not identifiers like table or column names or ASC/DESC — those must come from an allowlist. ORMs are safe by default, but their raw-query escape hatches are not.
questions.simple: Parameters are like filling a form: the user writes in the boxes, but cannot rewrite the form's questions.

explain.p: With pg, the query text and values are sent separately in the extended protocol, so the server never parses the value as SQL. With mysql2, `execute()` uses a prepared statement; `query()` with `?` escapes values on the client side, which is also safe for values but is a different mechanism.

explain.caption: Values use placeholders; identifiers come only from a fixed map

list: Prisma: `prisma.$queryRaw` used as a tagged template turns every interpolated value into a parameter, so it is safe. `$queryRawUnsafe` with a string you built yourself is not.
Knex: `knex.raw('... where id = ?', [id])` is safe; interpolating into the string is not.
Sequelize: use `replacements` or `bind` with `sequelize.query`, never template strings with user input.
LIKE: placeholders stop injection, but `%` and `_` in input still act as wildcards. Escape them if the user should not control the pattern.

explain.note: Defense in depth: the app's DB user should have only the permissions it needs (no DROP, no superuser), and pg does not allow multiple statements in a parameterized query, which limits damage.

followups.q: Is escaping input with a function as good as parameters?
followups.a: It is much more fragile: it depends on encoding, quoting context and getting every call right. Parameters separate code from data by design. Use escaping only for identifiers, with a library function like pg-format's %I, and prefer allowlists.

followups.q: Can stored data cause injection later?
followups.a: Yes — second-order injection. Data saved safely can be concatenated into SQL later by another piece of code. Every query must be parameterized, not just the ones handling request input.

followups.q: Does an ORM make you immune?
followups.a: Mostly, for normal query APIs. Raw queries, dynamic where-objects built from user JSON, and passing user input as column names can still be exploited.

mistakes: Using template strings with ${} for values in SQL.
Trying to pass a column name or sort direction as a $1 parameter.
Assuming input validation alone prevents injection.
Using $queryRawUnsafe or sequelize.literal with user input.

questions.title: Transactions in code
questions.question: How do you run a database transaction correctly with a connection pool in Node?
questions.short: A transaction lives on one connection, so you must check out a single client with pool.connect() and run BEGIN, your queries and COMMIT on that same client. Wrap it in try/catch/finally: on any error run ROLLBACK and rethrow, and always release the client in finally. Using pool.query for each statement is a bug, because each call may go to a different connection. Keep transactions short and never wait on external calls inside them.
questions.simple: A transaction is one phone call to the database. You cannot start it on one phone and finish it on another, and you must hang up at the end.

explain.p: `BEGIN` affects the session on one connection. If you run `pool.query('BEGIN')`, then `pool.query('UPDATE ...')`, the second call may run on a different connection that is not in a transaction at all, and the first connection is returned to the pool mid-transaction.

explain.caption: Passing a truthy value to release() tells pg to close the client instead of returning it to the pool

explain.note: Every code path must release exactly once. Releasing twice throws an error in pg; never releasing leaks the connection. A finally block is the simplest way to get this right.

list: Keep transactions short. Locks are held until COMMIT/ROLLBACK; a slow transaction blocks other writers.
Never call an external HTTP API or wait for user input inside a transaction.
Run the statements sequentially with await. Firing them in parallel on one client just queues them and makes error handling confusing.

ORMs have the same idea: `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)`, `sequelize.transaction(async (t) => ...)`, `knex.transaction(async (trx) => ...)`. Use the `tx` object for every query inside, not the global client.
Default isolation in Postgres and MySQL InnoDB differs (Read Committed vs Repeatable Read). Know which one you run on.

anim.title: A transfer that fails halfway is rolled back

steps.note: transfer(A, B, 30) is called. A has 100, B has 50.
Check out one client. Every statement of this transaction must use it.
BEGIN starts a transaction on c1 only.
Debit A. The change is visible inside this transaction but not yet to others.
Credit B. Both changes are still pending.
COMMIT makes both changes visible together. Either both happen or neither.
finally releases c1 back to the pool, ready for the next request.
Second call: transfer(A, C, 20). BEGIN, then A is debited to 50 inside the transaction.
Crediting C fails, for example a constraint violation. The await throws.
catch runs ROLLBACK. The pending debit of A is thrown away, so no money disappears.
finally still runs and releases c2. Then the error is rethrown to the caller.

followups.q: What happens if you forget ROLLBACK and just release the client?
followups.a: The connection goes back to the pool still inside an aborted transaction. The next user of that connection gets errors like 'current transaction is aborted' or, worse, runs inside someone else's open transaction.

followups.q: What is a savepoint?
followups.a: SAVEPOINT name inside a transaction lets you roll back part of it (ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name) without aborting everything. ORMs use it for nested transactions.

followups.q: How do you handle serialization failures?
followups.a: With SERIALIZABLE or REPEATABLE READ isolation, Postgres can abort with code 40001. The correct response is to retry the whole transaction function from BEGIN, a few times with backoff.

mistakes: Calling pool.query("BEGIN") and then pool.query for the rest.
Releasing the client only on success, leaking it on errors.
Doing slow network calls inside a transaction while holding row locks.
Running Promise.all on queries inside one transaction client.

questions.title: The N+1 query problem
questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem? How does it show up with Prisma, Sequelize or Mongoose, and how do you fix it?
questions.short: N+1 is when you run one query to get a list, then one more query per item to load related data: 1 + N round trips. Each is fast, but 100 items means 101 queries and latency adds up. Fix it by loading relations in bulk: Prisma include or select, Sequelize include (a JOIN), Mongoose populate (one $in query per path), a manual WHERE id IN (...) and a Map, or a DataLoader that batches lookups in the same tick. Spot it with query logging and counting queries per request.
questions.simple: It is like going to the shop once for a shopping list, then going back separately for each item on it, instead of buying everything in one trip.

list: A loop with `await` inside that calls the DB.
Lazy loading in ORMs: accessing `post.getAuthor()` (Sequelize) or a relation in a serializer for each item.
GraphQL resolvers that load a field per parent object.

explain.p: When lookups happen in many places (GraphQL resolvers, nested services), a DataLoader collects all `.load(id)` calls made in the same tick and runs one batch query. Create one loader per request so its cache does not leak data between users.

list: A JOIN with several one-to-many includes multiplies rows (posts × comments × tags). Sometimes separate batched queries are faster.
Only include what you need. `include: { author: true }` pulls every author column; `select` is lighter.

explain.note: Detect N+1 by logging queries per request in development (Prisma `log: ['query']`, Sequelize `logging`, `mongoose.set('debug', true)`) and in production via APM traces that show many identical short queries.

anim.title: 1 + N queries vs 2 queries

steps.note: One query loads 3 posts. So far so good.
The loop awaits a user lookup for post 1. That is a full round trip to the DB.
Post 2 needs another round trip, even though it is a tiny query.
Post 3 has the same author as post 1, but we query again anyway. 4 queries for 3 posts: 1 + N.
With 100 posts and 2 ms per round trip, that is about 200 ms of waiting just for authors.
The fix: include the relation. Prisma loads all posts first.
Then one batched query for all needed authors (or a JOIN, depending on the load strategy).
Prisma stitches authors onto posts in memory. 2 queries no matter how many posts.

followups.q: Does Prisma batch findUnique calls automatically?
followups.a: Prisma has a built-in dataloader that batches findUnique calls made in the same tick, for example inside Promise.all. A sequential for loop with await is not the same tick, so it still runs N queries.

followups.q: Is Mongoose populate an N+1?
followups.a: Not per document: populate collects all referenced ids and runs one find with $in per populated path. It is still an extra round trip per path, and deep nested populates can get expensive.

followups.q: When is a JOIN worse than two queries?
followups.a: When joining multiple one-to-many relations, the row count multiplies and the same parent data is sent many times. Two or three batched queries can transfer far less data.

mistakes: Awaiting DB calls inside a for loop over results.
Fixing N+1 by including every relation everywhere, fetching far too much data.
Sharing a DataLoader across requests, leaking cached data between users.

questions.title: ORM vs query builder vs raw SQL
questions.question: How do you choose between an ORM, a query builder and raw SQL in a Node project?
questions.short: An ORM (Prisma, TypeORM, Sequelize, Mongoose) maps tables to models and gives relations, migrations and types quickly, but hides the SQL, makes complex queries awkward and can generate inefficient queries. A query builder (Knex, Kysely) composes SQL in code with safe parameters and dynamic conditions while staying close to SQL. Raw SQL with pg or mysql2 gives full control and performance but you write mapping and types yourself. Many teams use an ORM for CRUD and drop to raw SQL for reports and hot paths.
questions.simple: An ORM is an automatic car, a query builder is a manual car with good assists, and raw SQL is driving stick on a track — more control, more effort.

list: ORMs make it easy to load too much (whole rows, deep relations). Always select what you need on hot paths.
Learn to read the SQL your ORM generates: turn on query logging and check it with EXPLAIN.
Know the escape hatch and its safe form (Prisma `$queryRaw` tagged template, Knex `raw` with bindings).
Migrations: Prisma and TypeORM generate them from models; Knex and Kysely have migration runners; with raw SQL use a tool like node-pg-migrate.

explain.note: There is no single right answer. A senior answer names the trade-off and says how you would mitigate it, for example: Prisma for the app, raw SQL for the reporting module, all reviewed with query logs.

followups.q: Why might an ORM be slower?
followups.a: Extra abstraction cost per query is usually small. The real cost is in the queries it generates: over-fetching, N+1 from lazy loading, or inefficient joins you did not notice.

followups.q: Where does Drizzle fit?
followups.a: Drizzle is a TypeScript ORM with a SQL-like API: schema in TS, queries that look close to SQL, and type inference. It sits between a classic ORM and a query builder.

followups.q: How do you keep raw SQL maintainable?
followups.a: Keep queries in a data-access module, name them, test them against a real database, and type their results. Never scatter SQL strings through route handlers.

mistakes: Treating the ORM as a black box and never looking at generated SQL.
Writing raw SQL with string concatenation to avoid ORM limitations.
Picking an ORM and refusing to ever use raw SQL even for complex reporting queries.

questions.title: Indexes and EXPLAIN
questions.question: An endpoint is slow and you suspect the database. How do you find and fix the slow query as a Node developer?
questions.short: First confirm it is the DB: time the query in logs or APM traces. Then run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the exact query with real parameters and look for sequential scans on big tables, large row estimates vs actuals, and sorts or nested loops over many rows. Usually the fix is an index that matches the WHERE and ORDER BY columns — composite indexes in the right column order — or rewriting the query so it can use one, like not wrapping the column in a function. Indexes speed reads but slow writes and cost space, so add them for real queries, not by guess.
questions.simple: An index is the index at the back of a book. Without it you read every page to find a word. EXPLAIN tells you whether the database used the index or read the whole book.

list: APM / tracing shows time per DB span in a request.
Postgres `pg_stat_statements` lists the queries with the most total time; `log_min_duration_statement` logs slow ones. MySQL has the slow query log.
ORM query logging in development to see the actual SQL.

explain.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, total FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'paid'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Before:
-- Limit (actual time=410.2..410.3 rows=20)
--   -> Sort (Sort Key: created_at DESC)
--     -> Seq Scan on orders (rows=2000000) Filter: customer_id = 42 AND status = 'paid'

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_status_created_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at DESC);

-- After:
-- Limit (actual time=0.05..0.09 rows=20)
--   -> Index Scan using orders_customer_status_created_idx on orders

explain.p: `EXPLAIN` shows the planned strategy; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and shows real times and row counts (careful with writes — wrap them in a transaction you roll back).

list: Composite index order matters: equality columns first, then range/sort columns. An index on (a, b) helps `WHERE a = ?` and `WHERE a = ? AND b = ?`, but not `WHERE b = ?` alone.
Functions on the column defeat a plain index: `WHERE lower(email) = $1` needs an expression index on `lower(email)`.
`LIKE 'abc%'` can use a B-tree index (with the right collation/operator class); `LIKE '%abc'` cannot.
Every foreign key you join or filter on usually needs an index (Postgres does not create them automatically; MySQL InnoDB does).
Index only the columns you query. Each index slows INSERT/UPDATE and takes disk and memory.
Low-selectivity columns alone (like a boolean) rarely help; combine them in a composite or partial index (`WHERE status = 'pending'`).

explain.note: In Postgres, `CREATE INDEX` without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes to the table while it builds. On a big production table always use CONCURRENTLY (and note it cannot run inside a transaction block, which matters for migration tools).

followups.q: Why might the planner ignore your index?
followups.a: It estimates a seq scan is cheaper: the query returns a large share of the table, statistics are stale (run ANALYZE), types do not match (comparing text to an integer), or the column is wrapped in a function.

followups.q: What is a covering index?
followups.a: An index that contains all columns the query needs, so the DB can answer from the index alone (Index Only Scan in Postgres). INCLUDE (col) adds extra columns without making them part of the key.

followups.q: Do MongoDB queries need indexes too?
followups.a: Yes. Use .explain('executionStats') and look for COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN, and totalDocsExamined vs nReturned. The same ideas about compound index order apply (equality, sort, range).

mistakes: Adding an index on every column "just in case".
Creating indexes on large production tables without CONCURRENTLY.
Running EXPLAIN without ANALYZE and trusting estimates that are far off.
Testing on a tiny dev database where everything is fast.

questions.title: Race conditions in app code
questions.question: Node is single-threaded, so how can you still get race conditions with the database? How do you prevent them?
questions.short: Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, but every await is a pause where other requests run, and multiple processes or servers run in parallel anyway. So 'check then act' across two queries is not atomic: two requests can both see 'no user with this email' and both insert. Push the guarantee into the database: unique constraints and handling the violation, atomic single-statement updates like UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0, or row locks with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction.
questions.simple: Two people check that the last seat is free and both buy it. The fix is that the ticket office itself refuses the second sale, not that each buyer checks more carefully.

list: Every `await` yields to the event loop; other requests interleave between your SELECT and your INSERT.
You run several processes (cluster, pods). In-memory locks in one process do not help the others.
Read-modify-write in JS: load a row, change a field in JS, save it back — the last writer wins and silently overwrites others.

explain.p: UNIQUE, foreign keys and CHECK constraints are enforced atomically by the database. Insert directly and map the error (`23505` unique_violation in Postgres, `ER_DUP_ENTRY` / 1062 in MySQL, `11000` in MongoDB). Or use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE` for upserts.

list: Lock rows in a consistent order (for example by id) to avoid deadlocks.
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` is the classic way to build a job queue table where workers do not grab the same job.
For MongoDB, use atomic operators in one update (`$inc`, `$set` with a filter) and unique indexes.

explain.note: A mutex inside your Node process only protects that process. Once you run two instances, you need the database (or another shared system) to enforce the rule.

anim.title: Check-then-insert lets two requests win

steps.note: Two sign-ups for ana@x.io arrive at almost the same time (double click, or two servers).
A runs the SELECT and awaits. While A waits, the event loop lets B run.
B runs the same SELECT. Neither has inserted yet, so both will see zero rows.
A passes the check and inserts.
B also passed its (now stale) check and inserts. Two accounts with the same email.
Fix: add a UNIQUE constraint so the database enforces the rule atomically.
A and B both just INSERT. A gets there first and succeeds.
B's insert fails with code 23505 (unique_violation). We map it to a 409 Conflict.

followups.q: Would wrapping the SELECT and INSERT in a transaction fix it?
followups.a: Not at the default Read Committed level: both transactions can still see no row and insert. You need the unique constraint, a lock, or SERIALIZABLE isolation with retries.

followups.q: What is SKIP LOCKED useful for?
followups.a: Work queues in SQL: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10 lets each worker grab rows nobody else has locked, without blocking.

followups.q: How do you avoid deadlocks?
followups.a: Keep transactions short, touch rows in a consistent order, and retry on deadlock errors (Postgres 40P01, MySQL 1213) since the DB aborts one side.

mistakes: Believing single-threaded Node cannot have race conditions.
Relying on an application-level SELECT check instead of a unique constraint.
Doing read-modify-write in JavaScript for counters and balances.
Using an in-process mutex when running multiple instances.

questions.title: Optimistic locking with a version column
questions.question: Two users edit the same record and the second save overwrites the first. How do you prevent lost updates without holding locks?
questions.short: Use optimistic locking: add a version column (or updated_at). Clients read the record with its version and send it back on save. The UPDATE includes WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 and sets version = version + 1. If someone else saved first, the version no longer matches, zero rows are updated, and you return 409 Conflict so the client can reload and retry. It holds no locks while users think, so it fits web apps where conflicts are rare.
questions.simple: Each edit carries a ticket number. If the ticket number changed since you started, someone else edited first, and you are asked to look again before saving.

head: Optimistic (version check)
Pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE)
rows: Conflicts are rare, edits span user think-time
Conflicts are common, short server-side operations
No — you cannot hold a DB lock between requests

explain.p: Return the version to the client, often as an ETag header. The client sends it back with `If-Match` (the HTTP-native way) or in the body. A mismatch becomes 412 Precondition Failed (for If-Match) or 409 Conflict.

explain.caption: A real handler would also distinguish "not found" from "version mismatch"

list: Mongoose: documents have `__v`, but by default it only guards array changes. Set `optimisticConcurrency: true` on the schema to check it on every `save()` (throws `VersionError`).
Sequelize: `version: true` model option adds a version attribute and throws `OptimisticLockError`.

TypeORM has `@VersionColumn()`, but it only increments the number: `save()` does not check it, so add the version to the update's WHERE yourself. Prisma has no built-in feature; use `updateMany` with a version in the `where` and check `count`.

explain.note: When the conflict is resolved automatically on the server (for example retry a background job), re-read the row, re-apply the change and try again a small number of times. Do not retry blindly with the old data — that just reproduces the lost update.

anim.title: Two editors, one version number

steps.note: Both Alice and Bob open document 5. They each read version 3.
Alice saves "Plan A" with version 3. The WHERE matches, so the row updates and version becomes 4.
rowCount is 1, so Alice's save succeeded.
Bob saves "Plan B" with version 3. The row is at version 4 now, so WHERE version = 3 matches nothing.
rowCount is 0, so we throw a conflict. Alice's change is not overwritten.
Bob reloads, sees "Plan A" at version 4 and decides what to keep.
Bob saves again with version 4. It matches, the update applies and version becomes 5.

followups.q: Why not just use updated_at as the version?
followups.a: It works if timestamps are precise enough and set by the DB, but two updates in the same millisecond or clock issues can break it. An integer version is simpler and unambiguous.

followups.q: What is a lost update?
followups.a: Two transactions read the same value, both modify it, and the second write overwrites the first without knowing it existed. Optimistic locking detects it; atomic SQL updates avoid it.

followups.q: Does Mongoose __v protect normal field updates?
followups.a: Not by default. Without optimisticConcurrency: true, __v only increments for certain array modifications. And findOneAndUpdate bypasses document versioning entirely.

mistakes: Checking the version in a SELECT and then updating in a separate statement (that is a race again).
Not checking rowCount, so conflicts pass silently.
Assuming Mongoose __v gives full optimistic concurrency by default.

questions.title: Handling DB errors and retries
questions.question: How should a Node API handle database errors? Which ones do you retry and which do you turn into 4xx responses?
questions.short: Classify by the driver's error code, not by message text. Constraint violations are the client's problem: unique violation (Postgres 23505, MySQL 1062, Mongo 11000, Prisma P2002) becomes 409, foreign key or check violations become 400/409/422. Transient errors — serialization failures (40001), deadlocks (40P01, MySQL 1213), connection resets, pool timeouts — can be retried a few times with exponential backoff and jitter, retrying the whole transaction, and only when the operation is idempotent. Everything else is a 500, logged with context but never leaked to the client.
questions.simple: Some failures mean "your request is wrong" — tell the user. Some mean "bad luck, try again" — retry quietly. The rest mean "we have a bug" — log it and apologise.

explain.caption: pg errors expose code, constraint, table and detail. Do not send detail to clients — it can contain data

list: Retry only transient errors, a small number of times (2–3), with exponential backoff plus random jitter so retries do not stampede.
Retry the whole unit of work — the full transaction from BEGIN — never just the failed statement.
Only retry when it is safe: idempotent operations, or ones inside a transaction that was rolled back.
Do not retry on a timeout where you do not know if the write committed, unless the operation is idempotent.
Do not stack retries at every layer (driver, ORM, service, client). Retries multiply and can overload a struggling DB.

explain.note: Pool connection timeouts under load are a sign of saturation. Retrying them immediately adds more load. Prefer failing fast with 503 and letting the client back off.

anim.title: A transaction retried after a serialization failure

steps.note: reserveSeat runs inside a transaction, wrapped by withRetry with 3 attempts.
Attempt 1 conflicts with another transaction touching the same rows. Postgres aborts it with 40001.
40001 is in RETRYABLE and we have attempts left, so we do not rethrow.
Wait about 100–150 ms (backoff with jitter) so the competing transaction can finish.
Attempt 2 runs the whole transaction again from BEGIN, with fresh reads, and commits.
The result is returned to the caller as if nothing happened.
Another call fails with 23505 (duplicate). It is not retryable, so it is thrown at once and mapped to 409.

followups.q: Why add jitter to backoff?
followups.a: Without it, many clients that failed together retry at exactly the same moments and collide again. Random jitter spreads them out.

followups.q: How do you know a write committed if the connection dropped during COMMIT?
followups.a: You do not. Design for it: make the operation idempotent (unique request id, upserts), or check the state before retrying.

followups.q: Should you match on error messages?
followups.a: No. Messages change between versions and locales. Use SQLSTATE codes (pg err.code), MySQL err.code/errno, Mongo err.code, or Prisma's error codes.

mistakes: Returning 500 for duplicate keys instead of 409.
Sending raw DB error messages (with table names and values) to clients.
Retrying a single failed statement inside an aborted transaction.
Retrying non-idempotent operations after an ambiguous timeout.

questions.title: MongoDB and Mongoose essentials
questions.question: What should a Node developer know about using MongoDB with Mongoose — schemas, lean(), indexes and common pitfalls?
questions.short: MongoDB is schemaless, so Mongoose adds schemas for validation, defaults, casting and middleware. Queries return full Mongoose documents with change tracking; for read-only paths use .lean() to get plain objects, which is faster and uses less memory but drops virtuals, getters and save(). Define indexes in the schema to match your queries, and check them with explain(). Remember that unique: true creates an index, not a validator, and that update queries skip validators unless you ask for them.
questions.simple: Mongoose is a strict receptionist in front of a flexible filing cabinet. lean() means "just give me the papers, skip the fancy folder".

list: Hydrating full documents is costly: each result becomes a Mongoose document with change tracking. lean() skips that.
Trade-off: no `save()`, no virtuals or getters (unless you add plugins), and ObjectIds stay as ObjectId instances.
Use lean() for API reads; use full documents when you will modify and `save()`.
`unique: true` builds a unique index; it is not a validation rule. Duplicates surface as a MongoServerError with code 11000.

Indexes are built by `autoIndex` on startup by default. In production many teams turn it off and create indexes through migrations or `syncIndexes()` deliberately, because building indexes on big collections is heavy.
`findOneAndUpdate`/`updateOne` do not run schema validators unless `runValidators: true`, and they skip `save` middleware.
Invalid ObjectId strings throw a `CastError`. Validate ids at the edge and return 400 (or 404).
Query filters from user input can contain operators like `{ $ne: null }`. Validate types, or enable `mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter', true)`.
Unbounded arrays inside documents grow toward the 16 MB document limit and make updates slow. Use a separate collection for things that grow without limit.

explain.note: Mongoose buffers commands while not connected, so a query can hang until `bufferTimeoutMS` (10 s by default) instead of failing fast. Await `mongoose.connect()` before starting the HTTP server.

followups.q: How do you do a transaction in MongoDB?
followups.a: Multi-document transactions need a replica set (or sharded cluster). In Mongoose: const session = await mongoose.startSession(); await session.withTransaction(async () => { ... pass { session } to each operation ... }); then session.endSession().

followups.q: populate vs $lookup?
followups.a: populate runs separate queries from Node and stitches results. $lookup is a server-side join in an aggregation pipeline. $lookup avoids extra round trips; populate is simpler and works with Mongoose models.

followups.q: How do you check index use?
followups.a: Call .explain('executionStats') on the query and check for IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, and how many docs were examined vs returned.

mistakes: Treating unique: true as validation and not handling error 11000.
Never using lean() on read-heavy endpoints.
Relying on update queries to run validators and save hooks.
Passing req.body or req.query straight into a find() filter.

questions.title: Schema migrations
questions.question: How do you manage database schema changes in a Node project, and how do you deploy them without downtime?
questions.short: Schema changes live in versioned migration files in the repo, applied by a tool (Prisma Migrate, Knex, TypeORM, node-pg-migrate) that records which ones ran in a table. They run once per deploy as a separate step, not on every app instance boot, and applied migrations are never edited. For zero downtime, make changes backward-compatible because old and new code run at the same time during a rolling deploy: expand first (add nullable column, new table), deploy code, backfill, then contract (drop old column) in a later release.
questions.simple: Migrations are a numbered recipe log for your database. Everyone applies the same steps in the same order, and you never rewrite a step that was already cooked.

list: Each migration has an id/timestamp and is applied in order. A table like `_prisma_migrations` or `knex_migrations` tracks which ran.
Commit migrations with the code that needs them. Review them like code — they are code.
Development: generate (`prisma migrate dev`); production: apply only (`prisma migrate deploy`, `knex migrate:latest`).
Run them in CI against a real database to catch errors before production.
Rename a column = add new column → write to both → backfill in batches → read from new → stop writing old → drop old. Several deploys, never one.
Adding a NOT NULL column: add it nullable (or with a default), backfill, then add the constraint.
Do not drop or rename something the currently running code still reads.

Watch for locks: some ALTERs rewrite or lock the whole table. In Postgres, create indexes with `CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction) and set a `lock_timeout` so a migration fails fast instead of blocking traffic.
Backfill big tables in small batches from a script or job, not in one giant UPDATE inside the migration.

explain.note: Running migrations on app startup across 10 pods means 10 processes racing. Most tools take a lock, but a slow migration then blocks every pod's startup and health checks. Prefer a single pre-deploy job.

followups.q: Should you write down migrations?
followups.a: They help in development, but in production rollbacks are usually done by rolling forward with a new migration, because a down migration that drops a column also drops data written since.

followups.q: What if someone edits a migration that already ran?
followups.a: Environments drift: production ran the old version, new environments run the new one. Tools like Prisma detect checksum changes. Always add a new migration instead.

followups.q: Do you need migrations with MongoDB?
followups.a: There is no DDL, but you still have index changes and data reshaping. Use a migration tool (for example migrate-mongo) or versioned scripts, and handle old document shapes in code during the transition.

mistakes: Editing or deleting migrations that already ran in production.
Renaming or dropping a column in the same deploy as the code change.
Running long backfills inside a single migration transaction.
Letting every app instance run migrations on boot.
